claims.text: The applicable material regime contains more than five noble-metal elements.
Inhibited precursor mobility governs low-temperature formation of single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling restrict atomic diffusion during nanoparticle formation.
Restricted diffusion kinetically traps the constituent atoms in a random solid solution.
Stochastic principles govern formation of low-temperature noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
If atoms had more time to diffuse, diffusion would drive phase separation or elemental segregation.
Statistical randomness arising from incorporation of many elements dominates crystal-structure selection.
Atomic diffusion length during nucleation and growth is the key structural mediator.
Restricted atomic motion causes stochastic incorporation of diverse elements into one lattice.
A modest temperature hold or controlled slow-cooling segment can be used to increase atomic mobility relative to a rapid quench.
Temporarily enhancing diffusion will permit atomic rearrangement and increase phase segregation or elemental clustering.
The diffusion-enhancing intervention will increase phase separation or elemental segregation relative to the rapid-quench baseline.
The diffusion-enhancing intervention will change particle morphology relative to the rapid-quench baseline.
The standard rapid-heating and rapid-cooling baseline produces single-phase, statistically mixed noble-metal HEA nanoparticles with minimal elemental segregation.
High synthesis temperatures can promote uncontrolled particle growth.
Excessively high synthesis temperatures can cause thermal decomposition.
The intervention is applicable only below temperatures that cause decomposition or uncontrolled particle growth.
Persistence of the same single-phase homogeneous structure after a confirmed increase in mobility would falsify the proposed kinetic-mobility mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions require more than five elements, whereas the boundary states ≥5 components, inconsistently including exactly five-element systems.
